title: The Red Earth Weaver
subtitle: A July in the Central Highlands
summary: Vola is eleven and lives in Antananarivo, the capital of Madagascar. In July, when the highlands are dry and cool, she takes the long bus ride to her grandmother's village to spend a month at the loom. Her grandmother, Bebe Ranaivo, is one of the last weavers of the region who still remembers the old patterns — patterns her own grandmother said were maps and calendars and memory, written in thread. There is one old lamba in the house whose pattern Bebe has never been able to read. And this July, Vola is going to see it with new eyes.

paragraphs: Vola was eleven and lived, most of the year, in a small apartment in Antananarivo — the capital of Madagascar, which everyone she knew called Tana. Her mother worked in a bank. Her father was a schoolteacher. Vola went to a good school and spoke French and Malagasy and was learning English. She had lived her whole life in the city.

Every year in July, when it was winter in the highlands — dry and cool and quiet — Vola took the long bus ride south to her grandmother's village. The village was called Ambohimena, and it sat in a small green valley about six hours from Tana by taxi-brousse. Her grandmother, whom Vola called Bebe, lived there alone in a small red-earth house with a thatched roof. Bebe was sixty-eight. She had lived in the same house her entire adult life. And she was, though Vola had not really understood this before, one of the last people in her region who really knew how to weave the old lamba.

paragraphs: Vola arrived at the house on the first afternoon of July. Bebe was standing in the doorway, one hand up to shade her eyes. She had known which taxi Vola would come on because she knew the schedule the way she knew the tides. When Vola climbed the last of the path with her small backpack, Bebe smiled a wide slow smile and said, "You are taller. Come. There is soup."

Inside, the house was one large room and a small side room with a bed. The main room had a small stove, a table, two chairs, a low shelf of cooking pots, and, along the whole of one wall, a stack of woven lamba — the long rectangular cloths that Malagasy people wore wrapped around their bodies, or draped over their shoulders, or given as gifts, or, when someone died, wrapped around them for burial. The stack was neat and tall. Bebe had woven every one of them.

In the yard outside, under a shelter of woven raffia mats stretched over four wooden posts, was Bebe's loom. It was very big — as wide as Vola was tall, and about half as long again — and made of dark wood polished by generations of hands. A partly-finished cloth was stretched across it, held taut by weights of small round stones. The colors were red-brown, deep purple, and cream, with a black line every so often. Vola had seen Bebe at the loom before, but she had never been old enough to sit at it and try.

"This year," Bebe said, over the soup, "we will make you a lamba. Your first. You will start it, you will finish it, and you will take it home to your mother. Not fancy. A simple one. But yours. That is what this July is for." Vola was very pleased. She had wanted this for two years.

paragraphs: The first week, they only did the simple things. Bebe showed Vola how to sit at the loom — legs crossed, back straight but relaxed, weight settled. She showed Vola how to hold the shuttle. She showed her the motion of passing it through the warp threads, and pressing down the beater to lock each row of weft in place. She did not let Vola do very much at first. "Watch," she kept saying. "Watch first. Weaving is not something the hands learn. It is something the eyes learn. The hands only follow."

So Vola watched. Bebe worked on the piece already in the loom — a red-brown wrap with cream borders — and Vola sat beside her and watched every movement. By the end of the week, Vola could see what Bebe was doing even before she did it. Her hands began to want to move. Bebe smiled and said, "Now. Now the hands know. This is the moment. Sit."

pages.imagePrompt: Mike Mignola style for children: interior of the house, evening. Bebe (sixty-eight) has taken down a large very old folded lamba from a high shelf and spread part of it out on the table for Vola (11) to see. The old lamba is a warm cream color with a dense complex pattern of small red-brown symbols across it — geometric, ordered, but not obviously repeating. Warm lamp light. paragraphs: That evening, after they had eaten and cleaned the plates, Bebe took Vola over to the wall of stacked lamba. From very near the bottom of the stack, she pulled out a very old one, folded small. She carried it to the table and laid it out. It was long — nearly as long as the table — and pale cream, with a dense pattern of small red-brown geometric shapes running across it. The shapes were not repeating in the usual way. They were arranged in an order Vola could not quite see.

"This one was my grandmother's," Bebe said. "Her name was Ravaka. She wove it before I was born. It came to me when my mother died. My mother told me, once, that this lamba was different from the ones Ravaka made for selling. She said Ravaka wove it for the family. She said, this one carries something. And I would tell you what, my mother said, but Ravaka never told me. She only told me it was here." Bebe touched the pattern lightly with two fingers. "My mother said, if you ever understand it, you understand it. But she never did. And I never have. Sixty years I have looked at this pattern. I cannot read it. Something is here. I don't know what." She folded it again and put it away. "Sleep," she said. "Tomorrow, more weaving."

pages.imagePrompt: Mike Mignola style for children: interior of the house, morning. Bebe (sixty-eight, white headwrap) sits at the table with Vola (11). paragraphs: The second week, while Vola sat at the loom and slowly began her own lamba — a simple one, cream with a dark red border, which Bebe called good, sensible, honest — Bebe began teaching her the old patterns. Not to weave them, yet. Only to read them.

"Every family in the highlands used to have their own patterns," Bebe said. "Not many people know this now. Most of what people weave today is decoration — pretty, meaningless, sold to tourists in Tana. But the old lamba were not decoration. They said things. My grandmother taught me some. I have taught almost no one. There are perhaps six people in this region who know what I know. When we are gone, it goes with us. Unless someone learns."

She showed Vola. A row of small triangles pointing up meant hills, and each triangle was a specific known hill in the region — you had to already know which hills. A row of thin parallel lines meant a river, and the number of lines told you how many streams fed it. A diamond meant a house, and the position told you whose. A little cluster of dots was a herd of zebu — the cattle of the region — and the number of dots was, roughly, the number in the herd. A single dark line running across a piece meant a boundary, a fady — a taboo — a place you were not to go.

"They were maps," Vola said slowly. "Some of them were maps." Bebe said, "Yes. And calendars. And records of who married whom. And records of a good year, or a bad year. Some of them were promises. Some of them were warnings. A woman who wove a certain pattern into her daughter's wedding lamba was telling her daughter, do not forget the boundary. Do not cross into that valley. Or, remember the drought in the year I was born. Or, our herd was once bigger than this. The lamba were how people remembered, before there were many books, and before the ones who could write were more than a few."

paragraphs: Vola began to see the old lamba around the house differently. There were seven or eight of them in the stack that were old — thirty, forty, fifty years old — and now, when Bebe pulled one out and unfolded it, Vola could see the small language in it. A trip her great-uncle had made, once, to the coast. A marriage that had gone well. A season the rains had come at the wrong time. Bebe would read the cloths for her, patiently, at night, and Vola would look at the small shapes and try to remember them.

But Bebe kept coming back to the one at the bottom of the stack. Ravaka's lamba. The one she could not read. She would take it out every three or four days and look at it, and shake her head slowly, and put it back. "There is nothing in here I recognize," she said one night. "Some of the shapes I know. A triangle. A dot. But the arrangement makes no sense. It is not any place I know. It is not a calendar I know. My mother said, my grandmother said it carries something. But I have never seen what."

paragraphs: On a Wednesday afternoon in the third week, Bebe was down at the village well and Vola was alone in the house. She had finished her weaving for the morning and had eaten. She went to the wall of lamba and pulled out the Ravaka one and unfolded it on the floor of the main room, all of it. It was much bigger opened out than she had realized — nearly two meters long. She stood at the edge and looked down at the whole thing from above.

For a long time she just looked. She had been trying to read it up close — trying to find one shape, and then another shape, and see what they meant together. Up close it was small and dense and made no sense. But from above, standing back, the whole thing had a shape. The pattern, as a whole, made a picture. She saw it slowly, the way a picture emerges out of a puzzle. She saw a long shape running down the length of the cloth — winding, snake-shaped. She saw a cluster of small triangles bunched at the top, and a scatter at the bottom. She saw a single hard vertical line about a third of the way in from the left. She saw a small round mark, dark, near the center, that she had not really noticed before, off to the side, embedded in the pattern like a knot.

pages.imagePrompt: Mike Mignola style for children: close view of Vola (11) crouched now at the edge of the old lamba, one hand hovering over the small dark round mark near its center, the other over the long winding shape. Her face shows a slow realization — eyes wide, mouth slightly open. Warm midday light. Heavy ink outlines, flat shadows.
paragraphs: She stood there for a long moment. Then she went to the doorway and looked out. She looked at the valley — the hills that surrounded Bebe's small house, the winding stream that came down the middle of it, the low bunch of hills to the north where Vola had helped water zebu the year before, the scatter of small houses to the south where the neighbors lived. She looked back at the cloth on the floor. Then she looked at the valley again.

The pattern on the cloth was the valley. Seen from above. It was the shape of Bebe's own valley, woven into the lamba by Ravaka more than eighty years ago. The winding shape was the stream. The bunched triangles at the top were the north hills. The scatter at the bottom was the neighbor houses. The hard vertical line was the old boundary wall that still ran, tumbled, across the far edge of the valley. And the dark round knot in the center was — Vola thought — Bebe's own house.

paragraphs: Bebe came back a little later. She was carrying a clay water jar on her shoulder. She stopped in the doorway when she saw the lamba spread out on the floor of her main room, and Vola standing over it. She set the water jar down carefully by the door. She said, "What are you doing, my heart?" And Vola said, "Bebe. Come and stand here. Look at it from here."

Bebe came and stood beside her. She looked down. Vola pointed at the winding shape. "The stream," she said. She pointed at the triangles. "The north hills." She pointed at the scatter of shapes. "The neighbors." She pointed at the vertical line. "The old boundary. And this —" she pointed to the dark small knot in the middle — "this is your house."

Bebe did not say anything for a very long time. She stood with her arms crossed, looking down. Vola waited. She was, for a moment, afraid she had said something silly. Then Bebe knelt down slowly, with a small sound of effort, and put one hand flat against the cloth. She began to trace, softly, with one finger — the stream, the hills, the neighbors, the boundary, the house.
"Yes," she said finally. "It is the valley. It is our valley." She sat back on her heels. "Ravaka wove the valley. My grandmother. Eighty years ago."

pages.imagePrompt: Mike Mignola style for children: interior close view. Bebe (sixty-eight) sits on the floor beside the spread-out lamba, one hand still resting on the cloth. Her face is thoughtful and moved. Vola (11) sits close beside her, cross-legged. Late afternoon warm light through the door. Heavy ink outlines, flat shadows.
paragraphs: Bebe was quiet for a while. Then she said, half to herself, "But why?" She sat and thought. Vola sat beside her and did not interrupt. After a few minutes, Bebe said, more slowly, "My mother told me a thing, once. When I was young. I never quite believed it. She said, my grandmother — Ravaka — knew where certain things were, in the valley. Certain marker stones. Certain old resting places of family who had died in her mother's time. Things that people had begun, then, to hide. Because the French administration had been coming through the villages and cataloguing everything and moving things. So the old markers were kept quiet. Ravaka knew where they were. My mother said she was told, but she was told a child — she never remembered properly. She always thought her mother told her too young. She said the knowledge was lost with Ravaka. She was sad about it."
Bebe looked at the cloth. "But Ravaka did not lose it. She put it here. In case someone came looking, one day, who could see. I never could see. Sixty years I had this cloth. My eyes were too close."

paragraphs: Bebe began, slowly, to read. There was a small knot of dark red thread off to the west side of the woven stream, embedded in the pattern like a bead. Bebe stared at it, and stared at the actual valley through the open door, and then she said, quietly, "There is a stone. Where the north path crosses the stream. A grey stone, split down the middle, sitting on its own by the water. Nobody ever knew why it was there. I have walked past it my whole life. My mother used to say, do not sit on that stone, it is not for us to sit on. But nobody knew why."

There were other marks. A cluster of three small pale threads on the south hills — Bebe thought about it for a long time and then said, "There is a very small mound there. Under a tree. It is nothing. It is just a lump. But it is always tended — always. My grandmother tended it. My mother tended it. I tend it. Nobody has ever said why we do. It is one of those things you just do." She looked at Vola. "I know why we tend it now. I have not known for sixty years."

pages.imagePrompt: Mike Mignola style for children: interior. Bebe (sixty-eight) and Vola (11) together carefully refolding the very old lamba. Their four hands work together on the cloth. Warm late afternoon golden light coming through the door. Heavy ink outlines, flat shadows, warm cream and gold palette.
paragraphs: They read it for another hour, together. Not everything — some of the small shapes Bebe still did not know. But she knew more than she had known that morning. When they were finished, Bebe said, "We will not go and dig anything up. That is not why she made it. She made it so the knowledge would not be lost. Not so it would be used. It is not for us to disturb what she was protecting. But now we know. Now the family knows again. That is what she wanted."
They folded the lamba carefully, together, and put it back at the bottom of the stack. Bebe patted it. She said, softly, in old Malagasy, "Thank you, Ravaka. I heard you."

Bebe (sixty-eight) sits nearby watching. Golden late afternoon light. Behind them the low green hills of the valley — the same valley now visible as a whole. Heavy ink outlines, flat shadows, warm cream and red-brown palette.
paragraphs: Vola finished her own lamba in the last week of July. It was cream with a dark red border, and Bebe pronounced it, seriously, a good first cloth. She said Vola had a straight hand and a patient one. She said Vola would come back next July and Vola would learn one old pattern — a real one. Just one. "I will teach you the pattern for your own valley," she said. "The one my grandmother knew. So it is not lost again."

On the last morning, Bebe walked Vola back down the path to the road where the taxi-brousse would come. She carried Vola's folded lamba for her. When the taxi came, she handed Vola the cloth. She said, "Tell your mother this is yours. Tell her — tell her that next July I will teach you the pattern of the valley. And in twenty years, when I am gone, you will still know it. And in sixty years, when your grandmother is gone, someone in this family will still know how to read this valley." She paused. "That is enough. That is what the weaving is for." And she watched Vola climb into the taxi, and lift her hand once in goodbye, and she stood in the red dust of the road until the taxi was completely out of sight.
